Still Alice is a quiet but devastating film about memory, identity, and the fear of slowly losing the person you once were. Directed by Richard Glatzer and Wash Westmoreland, the story follows Alice Howland, played by Julianne Moore, a brilliant linguistics professor whose life changes after being diagnosed with early-onset Alzheimer’s disease at fifty.

As Alice’s condition progresses, the film focuses less on dramatic moments and more on the small, painful changes that slowly reshape her world. Conversations become difficult, memories disappear, and the distance between her and the people closest to her quietly grows. What makes the film hit so hard is how human and restrained it feels, never exaggerating the illness, only showing how deeply it affects everyday life.

Julianne Moore’s performance was widely acclaimed for its realism and emotional subtlety, earning her the Academy Award for Best Actress. Based on Lisa Genova’s novel, the film also helped bring wider attention to early-onset Alzheimer’s and the emotional impact it has not only on the person diagnosed, but on an entire family.

At its core, Still Alice is about dignity, love, and the terrifying feeling of becoming unfamiliar to yourself while trying to hold onto the people who still remember who you are.
